title: Krishna fixes Radha's hair
hookLine: the love poem ends not with a wedding but with God fixing his beloved's hair
carry: in bhakti, god serves the one who loves
tomorrow: Arjuna asks which road is best

cards: A wedding. A kiss in the rain. Credits roll.
That's where a lot of love stories stop. Jayadeva's Gita Govinda ends somewhere much quieter.
After the hurt and the searching and the messages carried back and forth, after Krishna has pleaded with Radha to forgive him, she finally comes to him in the forest bower at night.
And in the poem's very last song, the morning after, Radha asks Krishna for something small. Fix my hair, she says. Put my ornaments back.

teach.b: Here is the Lord of the universe, the cowherd whose flute the gopis ran to, the child who showed the whole cosmos in his mouth, sitting in the grass, carefully drawing the line of dark makeup around Radha's eyes, pinning flowers back into her hair, fastening her anklets.
That's the poem's last image. Remember the line tradition says Jayadeva hesitated to write, where Krishna asks Radha to put her foot on his head? The ending finishes that thought.
On the bhakti road, God isn't only the one who is served. God serves. In the reunion, the Lord does seva for the one who loves him.
This week the karma road has been about seva: serving every being as God. In the Gita Govinda, God serves the soul.
The service goes both ways. The poem didn't stay on the page.

Tradition says its songs were sung in worship at the Jagannath temple in Puri, and temple dancers performed them; Odissi dancers still do. Singers perform its songs, the ashtapadis, each one built of eight verses.
And you can see this teaching in Hindu homes every morning.
Someone bathes the murti, the image of God in the family shrine, and dresses it: fresh clothes, flowers, a little jewelry.

teach.h: GOD SERVES THE ONE WHO LOVES.
teach.b: It's called shringar. Devotees read the poem's ending as the other half of that love: the God you dress and adorn is the God who once pinned flowers back into Radha's hair.

how: The Gita Govinda has long been sung in the worship of Jagannath at Puri and is performed in Odissi and other classical dance and music; in homes and temples devotees bathe and dress the murti each day (shringar), and hear the poem's reunion as God's love for the soul.

games.q: after the long night of reunion, Radha asks Krishna for one thing. what does she ask?
o: a promise never to see the other gopis.
to fix her hair and put her ornaments back.
to take her to his palace.
games.why: the poem ends with Krishna tending to her. devotees see God serving the soul, the way the soul serves God.

practice: Think of someone who once tended to you in a small, physical way: brushed your hair when you were little, fixed your collar before something important, brought you soup.
Picture their hands, and receive that care again as you breathe in. Then, if you keep a shrine, offer one small act of care today: a flower, a fresh cloth, a lamp.
If you don't pray, tend one person you love in a small way, as an offering.

wordCard.voice: Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry, and the Gita Govinda ends with a small, gentle action: God tending the one he loves.

orig.note: Sanskrit: 'eight steps': one of the Gita Govinda's songs, each built of eight verses with a refrain.

carryVoice: Your line: in bhakti, God serves the one who loves. The poem ends on flowers pinned back in her hair. That's day three hundred twenty-one.

sources.ref: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, cantos 11–12 (the reunion; Radha asks Krishna to arrange her ornaments)
